22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome

the syndrome is given; find the missing piece · calcium, T cells and microarray · which syndrome has which findingWhich component did the vignette leave out, and which bedside sign in the exam shows it?

1Illness script
Bottom line
  • A conotruncal heart defect with an absent thymic shadow, cleft palate or an abnormal face suggests 22q11.2 deletion; recite CATCH (cardiac outflow anomaly, abnormal face, thymic hypoplasia, cleft palate, hypocalcemia; 22 for the chromosome) to find the missing piece, often hypocalcemia.
  • Check ionized calcium and obtain echocardiography; confirm with chromosomal microarray or FISH (fluorescence in situ hybridization), not a standard karyotype.
  • Treat symptomatic hypocalcemia with IV calcium; until T-cell immunity is confirmed, give no live vaccines and only irradiated blood products.
What it is

22q11.2 deletion syndrome (DiGeorge syndrome, velocardiofacial syndrome): a microdeletion causing thymic and parathyroid hypoplasia with conotruncal heart defects.

Driver

Loss of the genes for third and fourth pharyngeal pouch development and neural crest migration.

Triggers

Usually a sporadic deletion; autosomal dominant when inherited

non-modifiable

Chain

22q11.2 microdeletion

third and fourth pharyngeal pouches fail

the thymus, parathyroid glands, palate, face and outflow tract all develop abnormally

T-cell deficiency, hypocalcemia, cyanotic heart disease

Insights

The stem often names the syndrome; the question asks for the missing CATCH component, usually hypocalcemia shown as a tremulous infant.

DiGeorge needs thymic involvement; facies and cleft palate do not have to be present.

Practice
  1. 3 h old F, cyanosis refractory to 100% oxygen, saturation 72% in right hand and leg, low-set ears, micrognathia, cleft palate, absent thymus on chest film, truncus arteriosus on echocardiography, tremulous on examination → Hypocalcemia → parathyroid hypoplasia in 22q11.2 deletion
  2. Term neonate with truncus arteriosus, cleft palate and an absent thymic shadow on chest radiograph → Chromosomal microarray for the 22q11.2 deletion → a standard karyotype does not resolve a microdeletion
  3. Neonate with known 22q11.2 deletion who develops a generalized seizure; ionized calcium is low → Intravenous calcium gluconate → hypocalcemic seizure from parathyroid hypoplasia
  4. 4 mo old with 22q11.2 deletion and a CD3+ T-cell count of 210/mm3, presenting for routine immunizations → The live attenuated rotavirus vaccine → live vaccines are withheld until CD3 and CD4 exceed 500/mm3 and CD8 exceeds 200/mm3 with a normal mitogen response
  5. Newborn with a double-bubble sign on abdominal radiograph, a single transverse palmar crease and an atrioventricular septal defect → Down syndrome → duodenal atresia
  6. Newborn girl with coarctation of the aorta, a webbed neck, wide-spaced nipples and a horseshoe kidney → Turner syndrome → 45,X
  7. Why the thymus, parathyroids, palate and cardiac outflow tract fail together in this syndrome → Failed third and fourth pharyngeal pouch development with abnormal neural crest migration → one embryologic field, four organs
  8. 6 yo with 22q11.2 deletion, recurrent sinopulmonary infections and poor responses to polysaccharide vaccines → T-cell subsets with quantitative immunoglobulins → humoral failure follows defective T-cell help
Decoy note Tremulous is the bedside sign of both neonatal hypoglycemia and neonatal hypocalcemia. An uncomplicated pregnancy in a primigravida with Apgars of 8 closes off the hypoglycemia route. The equal right-hand and leg saturations read as an incidental vital sign, but they exclude differential cyanosis, and with it coarctation and Turner syndrome.
Pearls Syndrome with a missing component: when a vignette describes most of a syndrome, recite the mnemonic and cross off what is printed. Answer with the remainder; CATCH, JONES and CREST are tested this way · Hypocalcemia and hypoglycemia share a neonatal presentation of jitteriness, tremor and seizure, and the pregnancy history separates them · Differential cyanosis means ductal or arch pathology; equal pre- and postductal saturations mean a fixed intracardiac shunt, which is what truncus produces · DiGeorge takes lymphocytes, so an option of neutropenia or anemia tests which lineage the thymus governs · Until normal T-cell immunity is confirmed, these infants need irradiated blood and no live vaccines · The same deletion has two names: thymic involvement makes it DiGeorge, and facial abnormality makes it velocardiofacial
Pairs with Congenital Heart Disease covers truncus arteriosus within the cyanosis differential, and the oxygen-refractory shunt logic that leads to it. Antibody Deficiencies covers the downstream question of which immunodeficiency the absent thymus produces. Ask: is the thymic shadow present, and does the face carry a syndrome? Genetic Syndromes Recognized at Birth places this syndrome beside CHARGE, VACTERL, trisomy 13 and Fanconi anemia. There, the deciding finding is the one on the fewest lists.
Transferable rule Read the last sentence before the vignette. When a vignette assembles a recognizable syndrome, the diagnosis is given, and the question asks for the component it left out. That component usually has a one-word bedside sign in the physical examination.
True-fact-wrong-slotHorseshoe kidney: a real and memorable syndrome pairing, but it belongs to Turner, and the equal limb saturations already exclude Turner's coarctation.
True-fact-wrong-slotDuodenal atresia: congenital heart disease with low-set ears reads as Down syndrome, but that is where duodenal atresia belongs and Down has no thymic aplasia.
Unchecked attributeNeutropenia: DiGeorge genuinely causes a cytopenia, but the lineage is lymphocytes; red cell and neutrophil counts are unaffected.
Mirror twinHypoglycemia: a tremulous neonate is the classic hypoglycemia cue and also the hypocalcemia cue, but this pregnancy was uncomplicated with normal Apgars.
